To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the chemokine receptor CCR5, which mediates HIV-1 entry into cells, is also expressed on the neuronal surface.
HIV-1 infection induces neuronal damage through activation of several pathways, including the NMDA receptor, chemokine receptors and inflammatory factors.

(1) HIV-1 infection of neurons leads to neuronal damage and death, and (2) the mechanism involves activation of chemotactic receptors (CXCR4, CCR5) and inflammatory mediators, leading to activation of caspases and other downstream mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification and validation of novel therapeutic targets for HIV-1 associated dementia (HAD), a neurodegenerative condition that is the most severe form of neurologic disease caused by the human immunodeficiency (HIV- 1) infection.

the identification of the molecular pathways involved in neuronal damage and apoptosis associated with HIV-1 infection, and the development of new therapeutic approaches for HIV-associated neurological disorders.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies to prevent neuronal injury in HIV-1 infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single mechanism of HIV-associated dementia.

HIV-1 infection is not the primary cause of HIV-associated dementia (HAD) but rather is an opportunistic infection that triggers the cascade of inflammatory and excitotoxic processes that lead to HAD.
HIV-1-induced neuronal injury is multifactorial in etiology and that the most promising therapeutic interventions will be directed at multiple pathways to neuronal damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-1 infection can activate multiple signaling pathways that lead to neuronal damage and death.
the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein, gp120, can activate multiple pathways to neuronal injury and death.
the chemokine receptor CCR5, which is a coreceptor for HIV-1 entry, is a major contributor to HIV-1 neuropathogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV-1 infection of neurons is not only associated with neuronal death but also with a variety of neuronal dysfunctions that are not directly linked to the loss of the cell.
the chemokine receptor CXCR4, which is activated by the viral protein Vpr and the host chemokine SDF-1alpha (also known as CXCL12), can induce neuronal death through activation of the NMDA receptor.
HIV-1 infection of the central nervous system (CNS) is associated with activation of multiple pathways, which may contribute to neuronal damage and death.
